operator. Despite this lack of self-adjointness, we demonstrate the 
existence of a unique elliptic finite-band Hilbert space and develop its 
associated Yosida approximation, all within the non-self-adjoint setting. 
Furthermore, we establish a non-self-adjoint version of Weyl's almost 
monotonicity theorem for the non-self-adjoint Diric operator, applicable 
within the non-self-adjoint Hilbert space.

The communication technology used in vehicular networks is a two-tier system, consisting of local vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communications and wide-area vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communications. Our research focuses on the analysis of a two-tier heterogeneous vehicular networks architecture that incorporates vehicles as relay nodes, with an emphasis on the effects of using vehicles as relay nodes. To model this architecture, a multi-level, multi-domain network based on Software Defined Networking (SDN) is proposed, that incorporates Road Side Units (RSUs) and Vehicle Relays Nodes (VRNs). Utilizing the flexible flows management of SDN, the network is viewed as a collection of sub-networks that are managed separately for the purpose of analysis. A case study demonstrates the efficacy of this approach by comparing the performance of two configurations, one with RSUs alone and one with both RSUs and VRNs, on a simulated road network. Results show that the second configuration outperforms the first, due to the improvement in network connectivity brought about by the vehicle relays. Furthermore, the SDN-based model allows for the isolation of specific network segments, enabling the network to adjust and respond to changing network conditions, such as the connection of new vehicles to the network.

Wikipedia's vast knowledge is comprised of over 50 million articles, yet only a minority are of high quality. The rest are plagued by inaccurate information, poor structure, and a general lack of reliability, making them off-limits to readers. Unfortunately, volunteers who edit Wikipedia can't pinpoint which articles need improvement, leading to their good intentions being wasted on already high-quality pages. To resolve this, we've developed a method that uses machine learning to automatically label Wikipedia articles with a degree of quality, saving editors time by directing them to struggling articles instead of irrelevant ones. Our research demonstrates that our proposed method is not only effective but also fair, with edit history factors contributing more significantly to predicting article quality compared to account-based factors.

One of the primary issues with adapting advanced software testing techniques to real-world applications lies in the significant expertise required to implement them. This issue can be attributed to various factors such as the reliance of these techniques on specific assumptions, the absence of transparent decision-making mechanisms and the inability to articulate reasons behind their recommendations. In this paper, we present a novel approach to address the aforementioned challenge by utilizing a black-box assessment framework that relies on the system under test providing input-output relationships instead of its source code. This framework is capable of delivering several benefits, including but not limited to the identification of the best approach to achieve a particular objective and the discovery of connections between targets that share no common data sources. Through the integration of mutual information-based encoding, the analysis of local patterns and the adoption of a decision-theoretic Baysian framework, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in transferring knowledge in a zero-shot manner without requiring any prior knowledge of the target system. This technique is capable of delivering accurate results that surpass the current state-of-the-art techniques, with a performance improvement rate of 110% and 23% respectively, in our evaluation studies.

The observed branching fractions for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0\bar{K}^0$ and $B^0_s\to
\bar{D}^{*0}\bar{K}^0$ decays were found to be $(5.2\pm0.6\pm0.3\pm 1.0) \times
10^{-4}$ and $(5.0\pm2.1\pm0.3\pm 0.7) \times 10^{-4}$, respectively, with $\bar{D}^0\bar{K}^0$ and $\bar{D}^{*0}\bar{K}^0$ denoting antiparticle combinations.

We apply the method of geometric t-duality to coordinate transformations representing twisted torus geometry, including the effects of Wilson lines. This method enables us to convert any t-dualizable configuration of the twisted torus into an equivalent one with a Wilson line, and conversely, to identify configurations that remain equivalent under geometric t-duality. Furthermore, this framework allows us to generalize t-duality to coordinate transformations that depart from standard form, while also incorporating the presence of charged fundamental strings.

A significant issue in the field of robot learning has been addressed in this research, specifically the challenge of training robots to collaborate effectively. We propose the concept of co-observation, which involves robots learning to perform collaborative tasks through observation of their counterparts, without the need for expert guidance. To achieve this, we have developed a novel approach called Specialization-Co, which enables robots to identify and learn from each other's skills. As a result, each robot can acquire unique abilities, enabling it to specialize and enhance its overall performance. We have demonstrated the efficacy of this method through simulation-based testing, which showcases its capability to facilitate successful collaboration among the robots.

PAC codes are recently proposed for reliable computation in fault-tolerant quantum computing. A key parameter, known as the terabit meter, in studying PAC codes, needs to be understood, which prompts this research. This paper, for the first time, provides a precise definition of the terabit meter and develops methods to calculate it for various types of codes, including matrix product codes, factor codes, and polar codes. Furthermore, this work investigates the methods for scaling up codes under weakly proper mortification, a concept introduced in this paper. These methods are demonstrated through the computation of crucial parameters, such as capacity, multiplexing factor, and error correction efficiency, in several examples.

In this work, we develop a novel approach for monitoring the engagement of objects with hands from a series of point clouds, an essential capability given the widespread availability of such data through various platforms like virtual reality head-mounted displays and 3D scanning technologies. To achieve this, we introduce the concept of 'temporally-consistent' 3D skeleton representations, allowing us to track the spatial movements and transformations of body joints over time. Based on this representation, we design a simple and efficient tracking algorithm for the 3D skeleton, which determines the state of hand-object engagements by analyzing the relative positions of hand joints and associated objects, also enabling the detection of new objects being grasped. Through extensive testing on a large, diverse real-world dataset, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods on all evaluation metrics, also exploring and revealing the biases of current hand-tracking algorithms within this dataset. Furthermore, we utilize our approach to analyze the standard benchmarks in the field, providing new insights and perspectives on current evaluation methods.

A type of C-collection known as a tail-triangle C-collection, specifically one with a rank of 4 and an interleaving number of 2, is defined by a set of 5 elements in a D4 lattice. This type of C-collection is used to count the possible shellings of a 20-element polyhedron. By analyzing the set's symmetry, the number of possible shellings is found to be 34440, after filtering out cases with too few faces. This count is consistent with the number of "good" shellings, obtained through a different combinatorial approach, confirming their equality. This research extends previous work in counting the shellings of a certain 20-element polyhedron by characterizing the sets that correspond to "good" shellings and showing they can be represented as rank 4, interleaving number 2 tail-triangle C-collectives. Additionally, the stability of the count for a related polyhedron, with 22 vertices and an interleaving number of 3, is confirmed through these C-collectives, also used to count its shellings.

A versatile, depth-sensing camera can be utilized on a robot for object inspection by determining surface irregularities or to identify characteristics essential for grasping. To use this camera on a robot without a pre-calibrated setup, adjustments are necessary to align the camera with the robot's base coordinate system. A novel approach presented in this research employs machine learning to calculate the adjustment parameters, eliminating the need for manual calibration. Furthermore, the paper proposes a novel method using a low-level image processing technique to estimate the end-effector position of the robot, which is then verified through experiments using the Telemach robot system and a depth-sensing camera. The results indicate that the estimates made and the actual positions are closely related, showing that the system is capable of accurate end-effector position estimation without the need for pre-calibration, greatly simplifying the integration of depth-sensing cameras on industrial robots.

This paper investigates the problem of identifying treatment disruption in a specific framework where multiple treatments are given to the same units over distinct time periods. Our objective is to determine whether treatment disruption occurs by comparing its impact on a continuous outcome variable at two distinct time points. To achieve this, we define a test statistic that assesses the differences in treatment effects across various treatment periods using a linear regression model controlling for background characteristics and the treatment received at previous time points within a k-nearest-neighbors framework that accounts for spatial relationships. Under specific assumptions, our test enjoys particular advantages such as consistency, power behavior, and asymptotic normality, enabling us to establish critical values and facilitate practical implementation of the test through Monte Carlo simulations via bootstrap resampling. Ultimately, our results provide evidence of efficient identification of treatment disruption in a data set comprising information on 415 districts across Mexico's state of Chihuahiuani.

The possibility of neutrino emission through the annihilation of Dark Matter particles within a compact, dense object is being investigated. Specifically, it's anticipated that the neutrino emissions resulting from the annihilation of a Dark Matter particle into a pair of pseudoscalar mediator particles would be substantial enough to influence the object's composition. Consequently, this could make it feasible to utilize the object's composition to substantiate the nature of its constituent particles. Our initial calculations, carried out using the dense matter many-body theory framework at a finite temperature, indicate that the neutrino emissivities generated by the pseudoscalar mediator process are improved when the density of the object is taken into consideration, much like analogous findings related to vector mediator particles. Notably, the system's high density has a direct positive effect on the neutrino emissivity, which may potentially be sufficient to fully dissolve neutrons and deprotonate atoms within a compact, neutron-rich object over an extensively prolonged period.

The ongoing UNIONS project, in collaboration with CFIS, has conducted the most comprehensive weak-lensing survey to date in the Northern sky. This has resulted in 484.8 square degrees of high-quality data, critical for studying the galaxy mass distribution. To analyze this data, an advanced machine learning-based galaxy shape detection algorithm was developed, utilizing the JAVELIN framework. This algorithm leverages 30.72 microseconds of computing power to efficiently detect shapes in the CFIS dataset. The resulting data, after being advanced, contains 47 million detected shapes, which served as the groundwork for a groundbreaking approach to mapping the galaxy mass distribution. This approach utilizes the advanced shape detection to analyze the galaxy positions and their relationship with the galaxy mass distribution, as observed in the UNIONS/CFIS dataset. The resulting data reveals the galaxy mass distribution's significant impact on the galaxy rotation curves. This has enabled researchers to further their comprehension of galaxy rotation curves, as observed in the UNIONS/CFIS dataset.

This broad investigation centers around the widespread occurrence of certain patterns of non-zero squares in relation to two-dimensional grids of units. It involves analyzing the patterns of even and odd squares when the grid's size becomes infinitely large, capturing a significant portion of these square patterns, which stems from the work of Weyl's density theory from the 1930s. Building upon Kronecker's initial findings from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, our analysis provides a more precise estimation of the square pattern distribution, validating the initial results of Chudnovsky and Levenstein from the 1970s. To conduct this research, we drew heavily from the work of many mathematicians, incorporating their ideas into our framework and acknowledging their contributions, which often involved innovative approaches to estimating the distribution of square patterns through the utilization of the continued fraction expansion of real numbers.

We establish that for k-rational singularities, k-Du Bois singularities, and k-runged singularities, k can be less than or equal to 1. Furthermore, for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities, we explore the relationship between k and the critical period. Specifically, for k-rational singularities, taking the k-th root may change the critical period if and only if k is between 1 and 2, while for k-Du Bois singularities, it may change if and only if k is between 1 and 3/2. Moreover, we show that for k-runged singularities with k=2, the geometric fundamental group is equivalent to the algebraic fundamental group.

A type of collective quantum disorder known as Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless phases can emerge in materials with interacting spins, facilitated by the influence of temperature or magnetic field in three-dimensional systems. We have discovered Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transitions that can be triggered by either temperature or magnetic field in the LiCuO2 material. Moreover, our studies reveal that the crossover temperature or the magnetic field at which it occurs can significantly be influenced by the magnetic field's anisotropy or non-uniformity, thus providing a potential means to control it.

In certain cosmological scenarios, an unexpected dip in the neutrino temperature or a more complex distribution within the universe could be observed. Introducing axion-like particles into such a state, however, may not necessarily result in a noticeable deviation from expected neutrino behavior. Even within the most extreme of cosmic environments, the influence of primordial black holes and similar objects on neutrinos remains minimal. But, in a specific scenario where a heavy dark matter particle exists, the corresponding self-interaction could significantly impact neutrino temperature, effectively creating a'shadow matter' effect. A notable feature of this process is that while dark matter particles may become non-relativistic, neutrinos remain relativistic, leading to a distinct phase transition. A future neutrino telescope located near a primordial black hole could potentially detect the residual heat left over from the phase transition, assuming the universe's dark matter is composed of such particles. A noticeable detection, however, would require an exceptionally large fraction of dark matter composed of these primordial black holes. Even within the most extreme of cosmic environments, the influence of primordial black holes and similar objects on neutrinos remains minimal. But, in a specific scenario where a heavy dark matter particle exists, the corresponding self-interaction could significantly impact neutrino temperature, effectively creating a'shadow matter' effect.

Quantum error correction using the fault-tolerant approach employed in topological codes, particularly those classically simulatable, has sparked interest in developing more advanced methods for classically simulating quantum systems. The stabilizer rank, a fundamental concept in this area, needs to be enhanced to achieve this advancement. This paper specifically investigates the stabilizer rank of Gottesman, Ben-Yosef, and Naveh's magic state, showcasing that current bounds using quantum entanglement measures are suboptimal compared to classical conditions, and presenting evidence that the existing lower bound is not the best possible.

Employing the Tsallis holographic dark energy model, we investigate the holographic dark sector in a quintessence-driven universe. The model utilizes AdS space, represented by the Tsallis form of the Ricci scalar, to model dark energy. The paper examines solutions where the complex quintessence field is driven by a complex field with specific properties, and we analyze the impact of Tsallis parameters on the real and imaginary parts of the field. The paper further focuses on investigating shadow radii derived from the Tsallis model, using Thomas-Fermi profile and Schrödinger profile, and we discuss their implications in understanding the Tsallis form of the quintessence-driven universe.

The Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopy survey, with its unique broad view and dynamic perspective, has become a significant observation campaign for studying both stationary and moving celestial objects. Introduced in 2014, LAMOST's time-domain observation program was created to facilitate the research of variable stars and changing-look AGNs by tracking their physical changes over time. Conducted on the 4m telescope with a Wide Field Survey mode, which allows for 256 unique observations every time, the time-domain program has successfully obtained 504 unique frames and tracked 677 unique stars on 162 nights across four $K^2$ fields. Combining all time-series data resulted in 2264 spectra, each accompanied by 84 photometric observations, which formed a comprehensive database for analyzing variable stars and quasars. Four specific fields, including EGGRM 1, EGGRM 2, CLV, and LVT, were found to hold over 300 stars that display periodic variability, among which 218 have been identified as confirmed stars, including 130 that have been previously overlooked in LAMOST's previous time-domain fields. Furthermore, the fields contained 32 changing-look AGNs as well as 28 unique variable stars that display non-periodic patterns, all of which provide valuable resources for conducting future research.

True random number generation can be facilitated by utilizing the inherent randomness caused in memory cells during under-volting, resulting in stable and reliable data collection with minimal physical mechanisms. This proposal, called TuRaN, entails a novel approach to harnessing randomness from under-volted SRAMs, using a significantly reduced number of bits to extract unique and unpredictable data, thereby enhancing the randomness extraction capability per clock cycle. Moreover, TuRaN's architecture allows for the integration of a minimal number of external components, thus making it an extremely resource-efficient solution for true random number generation. This method also possesses the capability to automatically adjust its operating parameters in response to process variations and utilize the inherent characteristics of the underlying PVT conditions, making it a highly adaptable system. This proposal is unique in that it separates itself from traditional SRAM undervolving methods, which prioritize minimizing failure rates in the context of reliable data retrieval.

A preliminary investigation of molecular nonvolatile single-electron resistive relays has been carried out, focusing on developing an accurate model to simulate this novel device concept. Initially, an idealized single-electron resistive relay is described, alongside a proposed architecture that incorporates two nonvolatile single-electron transistors. To this theoretical foundation, a microscopic model is added to improve the simulation's accuracy, taking into account the influence of a nonuniform dielectric environment on charge transport. The results obtained from these simulations predict that single-electron resistive relays can operate at relatively high temperatures, with the added benefit of being resistant to radiation, as the traps caused by irradiation can be easily overcome by applying a negative voltage to the gate. Furthermore, we have discovered that an optimized design can achieve a significant reduction in the required gate voltage, below 1 volt, necessary to operate the device at a desirable temperature.

We develop a novel numerical approach for evaluating multi-loop Feynner diagrams, incorporating innovations such as a creative expression of integrals, innovative integration techniques, and a groundbreaking method for comparing function values. The method is developed in a way that's completely independent of parameters, allowing it to efficiently compute self-energy and scattering processes with up to three particles. The technique has a known limitation of being unable to directly obtain analytical expressions, but it offers a promising solution for parameter-space integrations that could be applied to a broad range of phenomena, from particle physics to condensed matter and complex materials.

We've developed an expression that relates the time-dependent wave function of a two-state quantum system with a short period and a non-zero gap to the exponential of the Hamiltonian matrix multiplied by time: $U(t)\delta_{i,j}\to e^{-(\omega+i0)t}\delta_{i,j}$. This implies that for a diagonal initial condition, the system's wave function extends equally in both positive and negative time. We derive a general formula for the system's wave function using this principle and a corresponding formula for the bound states of a one-dimensional qubit system coupled to a harmonic oscillator. The formula shows that the bound states of the combined qubit-oscillator system can be extended to longer periods by appropriately engineering the coupling between the qubit and oscillator.

This study explores the possibility of existence of hybrid celestial bodies, comprising of quark and nucleon matter, within the framework of the $\Sigma$-$\Omega$-$\Rh$ model, in conjunction with the MJJ and NJL models. To investigate the mass relationship of these objects, we consider the mass gap equation and detailed mass transition processes. Furthermore, the study examines the potential for hybrid stars composed of quark and nucleon matter to undergo further transitions into strange matter. To facilitate this analysis, we employed the $S$-$\Omega$-$\Rh$ model, in conjunction with the MJJ and NJL models, to derive the thermodynamic properties of the matter in $\beta$-equilibrium with its respective model. To conclude, this study has investigated the thermodynamic properties of hybrid stars comprising quark and nucleon matter, as well as their thermal stability.

This study explores the properties of light interaction with a mechanically oscillating mirror in an alternative form of light, known as $q$-deformed optomechanical systems. We examined the expected behavior of both fast and slowly varying light processes and discovered notable differences. Notably, the overall light transmission through the system can be high in both cases, but the factors influencing it differ significantly, depending on the value of the $q$ parameter. Furthermore, in the case of slowly varying light, the influence of this parameter has a more pronounced effect. To better understand these interactions, we applied the transformation method to build an effective two-wave model for $q$-deformed optomechanical systems. Our findings have theoretical implications for the development of highly sensitive sensors using $q$-deformed optomechanical systems.

In the Double-Rotors Model, the Double-Rotors Model's R-parity conserved sector is examined, specifically its structural and excitational aspects relative to the standard model's R-parity conservation sector. It is determined that in this sector, the matrix of R-parity operators is invertible, but certain R-parity scissors modes are found to occur at adverse R-parity values, resulting in a distinct set of R-parity scissors modes operations.

Thinning down a material to a few atomic layers can have a profound effect on a material's properties. This is evident in the changes that occur in ultrathin FeO/Ge pseudosstructures, where the FeO layer's properties are greatly affected. To understand these changes, researchers employed density functional theory, including spin-orbit coupling, to conduct a comprehensive study of the configurations and variations in ultrathin FeO/Ge layers. The study identified and explained the stable configurations, their magnetic properties, and the fluctuations that occur as a result of finite size effects. The analysis revealed that the materials' behavior is closely related to atomic layer arrangements, rather than simply being a result of geometry. The study provided a detailed explanation for recent observations of spin-orbit interactions in these layers, and predicted the occurrence of spin fluctuations in certain layers. The findings of this research can help in the design and understanding of ultrathin FeO/Ge pseudosstructures, where the unique properties of the FeO layer can be leveraged to create novel devices.

The behavior of particles undergoing laser cooling in an optical grid pattern is
complex and influenced by the grid's dissipative properties. This impact is
equivalent to a friction force felt by particles in the grid's nodes. This
dissipative effect also causes phenomena such as Brownian motion-like fluctuations
in the grid's thermal state and the occurrence of rare, extended particle migrations
in the grid's nodes. Numerical simulations have been conducted to investigate these
phenomena and the associated distributions of particles cooling on the grid.

This study harnesses trading volume data to unveil the hierarchical structure within the cryptocurrency exchange network. The findings reveal a three-tiered framework, comprising cryptocurrencies, exchanges, and periods characterized by distinct trading activities. The research also sheds light on the exchanges that occupy prominent positions within this network, comprising three types of nodes: densely connected islands (exchanges with high trading activity and a broad range of traded cryptocurrencies), the Bitcoin cluster (driven by BTC trading), and temporarily emerging exchange clusters (characterized by cryptocurrencies such as Ethereum and XRP). The research further analyzes the dynamics of this network, including swap operations, the rise and fall of dominant exchanges in different periods, and the exchanges that have sustained their reputation throughout the network's history.

The formation of particles from acidic compounds is a crucial aspect of atmospheric physics. The application of theoretical models to these processes has revealed significant discrepancies between simulations that include zero-point motion and those that do not. To resolve these differences, researchers used the Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics method to model the growth of sulfuric acid and water clusters. Their findings showed that the role of zero-point motion depends on the number of participating water molecules. The inclusion of this motion can lead to significant errors if neglected, particularly when reactive processes are involved.

We establish the completion of the space of pairs of Young tableaux, a key step in developing a compactification in the context of representation theory. Utilizing the exactness of certain categorical embeddings, we identify the closure of the discrete set of Dyck paths within the polytopal structure of injective embeddings of posets. This allows us to construct the compactification of the space of non-dilating operators for a finite reflection group of type A, B, C, D, E, or H by equipping it with a suitable topology that accords with its algebraic structure as a group of matrices acting on a vector space.

The relationship between thermal and electric currents in quantum systems exhibits unique characteristics that diverge from the analogous thermal and electric responses in general nonlinear susceptibilities. This distinction is evident in various thermoelectric devices and also holds true for certain quantum fluids undergoing rotation, where it contradicts expectations based on Einstein's relations. We have found that this contradiction stems from the breaking of spatial symmetry in these systems, which leads to the mixing of spatial and temporal components and thus violates Einstein's relations. This understanding may lead to the development of novel thermoelectric devices that utilize this property.

In various areas of neuroscience and machine learning, the preference of complex networks over simple ones has been extensively explored. We contend that the abundance of features in complex networks is the result of a hidden bias present in the data, which we have identified as the complexity itself. We have developed a new perspective on this issue and introduced a novel concept called Geometric Intricacy Regularization (GIR). GIR encompasses a wide range of biases, including overfitting regularization, which can account for the preference of simple models over complex ones. We have demonstrated that most current deep learning architectures act as a GIR regulator and proposed the Intricacy Asymmetry Regularization (IAR) to address this issue in the future.

We introduce a novel, fully inclusive approach to determine the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes by analyzing the $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decay and focusing on the $q^2$ dependence of its low-$q^2$ region (below 1 GeV$^2$). Our proposals rely on the use of unfixed $R_1^{K^*}$ asymmetry and $P_2$ plane areas, both of which exhibit $q^2$ dependence. In a Wilson coefficient fit, assuming seven Wilson coefficients are variable, our method enables the Wilson coefficient $C_9$ to be resolved with high precision even when influenced by uncertainties associated with $b\to s$ transitions. Additionally, our framework allows for the direct determination of ratio $R_{9}(2<q^2<6\,{\rm GeV}^2)$ with the data from $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays.

Recent advancements in transformer-based architectures have led to notable performance gains in music generation tasks, such as the dataset-based Compose-a-Scene challenge. To further improve this development, we identify areas of enhancement within the Compose-a-Scene dataset, a notable challenge in the MUSICOUGH dataset series. Through analysis, we determine that the current state of the dataset is deficient in certain aspects, particularly the presence of non-sequentially composed music, leading to difficulty in creating valid compositions. To rectify this, we propose to supplement the dataset with valid, sequentially composed music, utilizing transformer-based architectures for automated exploration. Specifically, we will integrate a set of note-level language models to guide the exploration, which is demonstrated to significantly boost the performance of human evaluators in the Compose-a-Scene challenge.

The use of copula models to analyze joint probability distributions has become increasingly popular due to their flexibility in simulating diverse distributions and their ability to express a distribution's marginal components through individual probability functions. This has led to the development of various methods to apply copulas in a marginal dependence framework, which can be categorized into three primary approaches: the parametric method, based on model parameters; the nonparametric method, using statistical estimation; and a third method, incorporating both, often through model validation. This article discusses the first two methods, while providing an overview of the third in future work. The text also includes the derivation of key expressions for assessing dependence in a marginal framework, to facilitate comparisons between alternative methods and approaches.

We present a framework for intergenerational mobility that accounts for the passage of information from one generation to the next and how opportunities arise and disappear over time. Our model features a sequence of events, with each event offering various career paths that yield different returns on investment, and it is known in advance how these paths will evolve. Individuals in our model make investment choices with the prospect of earning a good return in mind, and we show that their decisions are affected by the opportunities available to their children and descendants. This, in turn, leads to a distribution of wealth that is passed down through generations, taking into account the dynamics of how prospects change over time as well as the persistence of wealth from one generation to the next. We find that, as the level of information about future opportunities increases, the gap in wealth between different generations tends to narrow. Our model is then used to demonstrate the consequences of a divide between the "haves" and "have-nots" when it comes to access to information, as well as the impact of investments that are intended to benefit future generations through inheritance taxes.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining their statistical behavior, according to a theoretical framework. This framework reveals the connection between spin and statistics, allowing us to introduce spin formalism in a purely non-relativistic context. By defining wavefunctions and their angular momentum properties without referring to spin, we can determine wavefunction properties more easily. Furthermore, a simple, elementary proof of the spin-statistics theorem is developed within this framework.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, its association with a more secure DPoS consensus mechanism enables the preservation of notable properties such as transaction forwarding and public wallet address anonymity.

A new concept, called space toughness, is proposed to assess the robustness of solving systems of linear equations against malicious manipulation of matrix and vector data. By extending the idea of toughness from graph theory, space toughness provides a framework to measure the resistance of solving systems in various data formats and representations. Furthermore, space toughness offers a unifying approach to compare the robustness of different solver designs, such as those using gradient descent, matrix inversion, and quantum arithmetic. To evaluate this concept, several practical applications and experiments were performed to verify the space toughness of popular solver libraries for linear equations. The results show that popular solvers and libraries can be vulnerable to attacks, but taking space toughness into account can significantly improve the robustness of solving systems, often without substantial performance degradation.

The initial discovery of the dominant strong interaction process $pp \rightarrow W^+ W^- H$ was made utilizing the LHC's CERN particle detector, with the subsequent analysis of its associated triple-meson interactions $W^\pm Z H$ providing the primary focus of a specific investigation. With a luminosity of 137 inverse femtobarns, the specified observation of the $W^\pm Z H$ process was made at a 13 TeV energy level, with its creation rate observed to be 5.7 times more frequent than predicted by the standard model, incorporating a non-resonant account of the $pp \rightarrow W^+ W^- H$ interaction. Through a standardized statistical method, the $W^\pm Z H$ signal was observed to be consistently present at a 3-sigma level, with its newly set upper limit seen to be in line with the standard model's expected predictions, with the observed rates differing by approximately 10% due to differing mass assumptions. Additionally, the specified observation of the $W^\pm Z H$ interaction offers significant scope for further research into the Higgs boson's anomalous interactions, with potential constraints imposed on modified theories incorporating anomalous Higgs quartic couplings, with the $W^\pm Z H$ interaction proving particularly effective at detecting such anomalies due to its extensive production rate across a range of 1 to 2 TeV.

We introduce the second edition of the Hebrew Universal Dependencies treebank, 
enhancing the original dataset with more comprehensive coverage of written 
Hebrew by integrating annotated texts from various domains, including law, 
medicine, and the humanities. This updated treebank includes 26,111 sentences 
and 1,838,811 tokens, offering deeper insights into Hebrew's syntax and 
morphology. Additionally, our evaluation of dependency-based parsing models 
reveals significant room for improvement in handling non-biblical, 
comprehensible text, and the full Hebrew corpus, and we identify specific 
challenges associated with these tasks.

We establish that for any two elements $A, B$ within the domain of $\ell_p$ where $1 < p < \infty$, and $\varepsilon$ within the range $0 < \varepsilon < 1$, if there is a bijective mapping $\Phi: A \to B$ that maintains $\| \Phi x \|_p \leq (1 + \varepsilon) \| x \|_p$ for all $x \in A$, then $\Phi$ can be extended to a linear map $T: \ell_p \to \ell_p$ such that $\| T x \|_p \leq (1 + \varepsilon) \| x \|_p$ for all $x \in \ell_p$, and this new map $T$ retains $\varepsilon$-isometry on incompressible subsets of $\ell_p$ including $A$. Additionally, $T$ is also known to be $\varepsilon$-isometric on $A$ itself. The $\ell_p$-isometry map $T$ is also shown to preserve incompressibility for all incompressible subsets of $\ell_p$ with $1 < p < \infty$.

Recent advancements in collaborative learning have made it possible for multiple groups to share data and produce enhanced results, however traditional implementations rely on the assumption that each partner has an equal contribution which isn't representative of real world scenarios. To overcome this, we have come up with a novel algorithm that doesn't presuppose equal involvement and can be easily applied to various types of models and learning tasks. Our proposed method has been successfully tested on models consisting of multiple layers and complex architectures, produced substantial gains in performance, and outshines alternative approaches significantly. To confirm that our solution is the optimal way to tackle this problem, we have developed mathematical proofs and confirmed these findings through thorough testing.

This letter presents the results of a thorough traffic analysis for a system that combines degree-degree connected low-density parity-check (DD-LDPC) codes in use at IP networks and a binary erasure channel (BEC). The study found that the output of the decoder enters a transient state characterized by frequent and temporary connections, which are then replaced by stable and sustained interactions. The time required to reach this transient state is shown to be affected by the density of the LDPC matrix and the number of bits sent. The work also reveals that the length of this transient state is influenced by the minimum degree of the LDPC matrix and the number of bits sent, and such designs should therefore balance density and the number of bits to minimize the impact on the network's performance.

For the proactive assurance of system safety, advanced monitoring and diagnostic systems are employed that use predictive maintenance to identify and fix potential issues before they occur. A key technique for realizing such a system is Prognostic Safety Solutions (PSS). PSS consists of two essential components: a predictive model for forecasting system performance and a procedure for calculating the timeframe in which a predictive failure might occur. This design provides the ability to adjust the lifespan of a system according to its operational requirements, thus enabling operational timelines to be aligned with operational budgets. A model-based approach for forecasting failure times is proposed, which is grounded in system level modeling and analysis, and is illustrated using an example from the aerospace industry.

A critical component in the decoy state approach for secure quantum key distribution (QKD) is determining the states' phases. However, if the phases of the decoy-state preparation process are not fully randomized, a potential attacker could exploit this weakness to manipulate the system and gain access to sensitive information. Our research specifically examines how a similar-technology attacker could compromise the system using a specific type of phase randomness known as partial phase randomness. To address this vulnerability, we also discuss how to enhance the system's security by implementing suitable key detection functions and increasing the rapidity of key formation.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated the effectiveness of "in-context" learning, where the model is not trained with task-specific data and instead, the desired task is performed within a short text context. Our research explores the impact of pre-training datasets on the performance of LLMs in-context learning methods across multiple tasks. Notably, we discovered that increasing the domain diversity of the pre-training dataset can enhance the model's ability to accomplish new tasks through in-context learning, specifically those from the same domain as the training data. Nevertheless, the model's performance in tasks from novel domains remains stable, regardless of the domain variability in the pre-trained dataset. Moreover, we observed that a substantial number of tasks from the OMCS-D dataset, originally outside the scope of the pre-trained data, can be learned through in-context methods, indicating the potential for future data augmentation to expand the model's learning capabilities to new domains.

Galaxy formations are significantly influenced by the interaction between galaxies and their surrounding gas, whether it's an existing galactic cloud or a galactic group's collective gas. This research utilizes computational methods to examine the processes of gas condensation and cloud fragmentation in galaxy clusters and groups, incorporating parameters like magnetic fields and thermal pressure. The simulation shows that when the kinetic energy of gas particles exceeds a certain threshold, typically around 10^3 pa ks, the fragility of galactic clouds significantly increases, leading to their breakdown and the creation of smaller clouds. The simulation also indicates that these smaller clouds are often spiral and wispy in shape, with properties more similar to those observed in smaller galaxy systems. Additionally, the simulation shows that when magnetic fields within the gas play a major role, the resulting clouds are denser and more irregularly shaped than in simulations without magnetic fields, with properties more similar to those observed in the Milky Way and other spiral galaxies.

The concept of CP transgression is straightforward - it occurs when beauty standards in physical laws differ from elegance in mathematical representations, leading to varying outcomes based on observation direction. Research has discovered instances of CP transgression in the patterns of snowflakes and the shapes found in quartz crystals, suggesting that their underlying structures may hold clues to the fundamental principles of nature. By analyzing these patterns, scientists hope to gain insights into the symmetries governing the laws of physics, with potential breakthroughs in our understanding of the principles of nature.

New bosonic scattering amplitudes for all combinations of four and ten boson interactions have been derived directly from superstring theory using a newly developed algorithm, which also yields amplitudes for fermion interactions in terms of boson amplitudes. Extending the algorithm to five-loop order has been proposed. The amplitudes are expressed through polylogarithms up to eleven-loop order, with the derived amplitudes for four-graviton and self-interacting gluon scattering matching predictions made by the S-matrix dual proposal of string theory, demonstrating a theorem by Gross for superstring theory. The amplitudes for ten-boson interactions, previously unknown, reveal a non-trivial pattern in the dilaton amplitude and the overall structure of superstring theory four-point scattering.

To effectively manage their resources, future cellular networks will employ a complex set of computer programs that interact with each other in a dynamic and ever-changing environment. Just like a living organism's core functions, these programs ensure the network's day-to-day operations run smoothly, thereby requiring efficient management through various processes. In our research, we are exploring strategies to seamlessly control the operation of these programs, minimizing disruptions and maximizing system availability during sudden changes in the network and its surroundings. To achieve this, we are developing self-regulating mechanisms that adapt to and predict upcoming fluctuations in the network, much like an automatic system that maintains a comfortable temperature. In our study, we specifically examined the dynamic behavior of resource management in cellular networks and discovered that processes influenced by random events can be difficult to predict and control. Ultimately, we presented various processes and environmental conditions that affect and interact with resource management in these systems, and identified areas where external intervention can be beneficial.

The objective of zero-speech voice synthesis is to create a vocal version of a language without any supplementary data or annotations. The approach we take involves using acoustic units as targets for a vocoder, with the units being identified and ranked in order of importance based on their occurrence in speech from listeners' descriptions. The synthesis of individual acoustic units is handled by a vocoder that makes predictions over short audio segments, with the quality of the output being evaluated using both a mean absolute error measure and a subjective test. The results from the objective error analysis indicate a significant improvement in the output of the system following the incorporation of speech from listeners' descriptions. The subjectively perceived quality of the synthesis also shows a notable gain, with the system being considered to produce high-quality speech that is comparable to a system trained using speech from a established corpus.

A novel method known as McCormick Self-Opt (MSEO), an iterative approximation algorithm, is introduced to establish a series of linked convex optimization problems at each step, each refining the previous solution within defined operational windows, thereby producing multiple staged optimizations. Each optimization stage is evaluated for its feasibility and an associated error measure, guiding the progression to the next stage. To accelerate initial problem formulation, MSEO incorporates a novel McCormick envelope data generator for coupled objective functions. The proposed method's performance is tested using a motion planning scenario and compared against established tightening methods for linked optimization problems under realistic computational constraints, demonstrating that MSEO's adaptive nature yields optimal or near-optimal solutions at each stage, thereby producing satisfactory motion plans.

We examine the constraints on transforming non-classical quantum states using probabilistic protocols, specifically the resource monotonicity principle in the context of resource theory. Our investigation focuses on indefinite definite entanglements, which can be freely created or destroyed, but cannot be extracted through probabilistic conversion. Conversely, we show that hypergraph states are subject to distinct resource theoretic treatments based on their degree and connectivity. Furthermore, we establish that hypergraph states can be manipulated via probabilistic protocols, although their convertibility is restricted by a hypergraph's underlying structure. Specifically, we identify the critical condition for probabilistic convertibility between hypergraphs, revealing that hypergraph connectivity plays a pivotal role in determining quantum state transformability.

Coffee, being a common staple in many people's lives, exhibits a notable
physical phenomenon where whipped cream tops swirl in a repetitive, rotating
motion. This process is driven by a force that acts against the swirling motion,
creating an interesting opposition that ultimately results in an appealing, 
spiral pattern seen in well-stirred coffee. To understand this pattern, the 
complexity of the system can be simplified by modeling the whipped cream as a 
pendulum, which is then subjected to an external driving force. The resulting 
theory is compared to observed data, which shows that this comparison holds 
precise value. The resulting equation is also used to develop a practical, 
experiment-driven method for determining the critical threshold at which the 
system transitions into the desired spiral pattern.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust decentralized learning problem by minimizing the conditional expectation of the Lagrangian function over the population. To achieve this, we employ a graph-theoretic approach with connected and geometrically uniform node connections. Our method, known as DR-DSGD, is an efficient decentralized optimization technique that runs in $O(NTT \log (N(T+1))/k \log (NT/k)$ steps, where T is the time horizon, N is the number of nodes, and K is the support set size. Our approach relies on the local availability of empirical conditionally reduced support (ECRS) samples, with each node maintaining ECRS samples from its neighbors using a spatially weighted graph. We prove our method's theoretical convergence and resilience in the face of adversarial attacks that manipulate the communication graph, with our analyses based on the mixed-norm smoothness and the geometric type of the Lagrangian function.

Relativistic nuclear collisions involving heavy ions produce a fireball that gives rise to charged particles observed in the event. The number of charged particles created is typically attributed to two factors: the energy released from the fireball, which is then transferred to particles, or the expansion of the fireball itself, which may pull energy out of the fireball and manifest as particles. While the energy from the fireball is relatively well understood, the second mechanism, known as 'pull energy,' is less understood. Researchers have discovered that relativistic nuclear collisions come equipped with locations where pull energy is generated, known as 'pullers,' that are characterized by negative values of the gradient expansion coefficient $\alpha_1$. The amount of pull energy is quantifiable via the initial condition energy, denoted as $E_{\text{i.c.}}$, which is calculated using the relativistic perfect fluid model. The $E_{\text{i.c.}}$ is dependent on the amount of pull energy and can be used to investigate its significance. The $E_{\text{i.c.}}$ is also used to normalize the yield of charged particles, thereby providing insight into how the pull energy influences the particle generation. The $E_{\text{i.c.}}$ is also used to investigate how it changes based on the collision angle and whether or not it varies significantly based on whether the fireball is moving quickly or slowly.
