We conducted a comprehensive analysis of the physical properties of young stars, including those associated with protostellar jets, using data from submillimeter images and spectral energy distributions. Our research focuses on the interplay between high-speed jets and low-velocity outflows in the early stages of star formation. High-speed jets are known to be a common feature in young stars, but it's unclear if they can also enhance or depend on low-velocity outflows. To investigate this, we selected 14 stars and obtained ALMA images at 1.1 mm, covering a 50x50 arcsecond area, to identify CO and CS branches associated with high-speed jets and low-velocity outflows. The analysis revealed that all targets exhibit both high-speed jets and low-velocity outflows, and we obtained key parameters, including mass accretion rates and gas outflow rates. Our results show that the following can be determined with ALMA observations: the driving of low-velocity outflows by high-speed jets; the dependence of low-velocity outflows on high-speed jets; and the associated mass loss in the early stages of star formation.

A fundamental problem in applied mathematics and engineering, the equilibration task, involves adjusting a parameter in a nonlinear system to counteract disturbances and maintain operations within safe limits, even in the face of limited system information. Due to the inherent complexity of many real-world systems, with their numerous variables and limitations on measurement capabilities, solving this problem is challenging. The good news is that, in general, restricted access to a system does not prevent finding a solution, although the outcome may depend on the specific system dynamics and available information. The bad news is that, in practice, accurately calculating the exact solution can be computationally infeasible, leading to the necessity of finding approximate solutions that are both easy to compute and effective in achieving equilibrium. The main contribution of this work is the development of an algorithm for finding an efficient, simplified solution to the equilibrated regulation problem for a particular class of nonlinear systems, which involves linear parameters, subject to significant uncertainty. The proposed method produces a solution that is easily implementable in practice and is proven to be capable of achieving equilibrium, with the distance between the resulting state and the desired equilibrium being bounded. The novelty of this work lies in the fact that the proposed approach is adaptable to various types of uncertainty models and can be applied to a wide range of systems with linear parameters, even in the presence of limited system information.

The Solar Radiation Pressure effect causes a small body in orbit around the Earth to experience a subtle gravitational pull, resulting in a phenomenon known as the Solar radiation pressure perturbation. To study this interaction, researchers often utilize the method of adjacent bookkeeping to identify and analyze the resonant interactions at specific frequencies. Within the framework of this method, a technique called the SSBA approach is employed, which aims to determine the boundary values that separate the regions of stability and instability. To validate the SSBA approach, researchers often rely on numerical integrations of the equations of motion, which however, require specific initial conditions to do so. To circumvent this challenge, this study presents analytical expressions for the boundary values, obtained by means of the SSBA approach, which can be effectively calculated in the case of the three classical frequencies of the small body. To further enhance the accuracy of the theoretical results, this study also presents an alternative numerical method, which enables the integration of the equations of motion in the case of arbitrary initial conditions, by expressing them as a combination of geometric series. To verify the accuracy of the theoretical results, this approach is compared with numerical integrations of the equations of motion in the vicinity of the (1, -1/3) and (2, -1/2) resonances, which demonstrates the efficacy of the method in the case of the (2, -1/2) resonance, but not in the case of the (1, -1/3) resonance, which

We employ measure-invariant techniques to analyze the discrete models derived from light-matter interactions using first-principles with a particular implementation of tight-binding models. Our methods involve discretizing the Schrödinger equation using finite elements and projecting the electromagnetic field onto a basis of vector potential planes. These approaches yield models dependent on the Lorentz degree of freedom and the number of electrons, making them non-relativistic and semi-classical. Our results from a silver d-d transition metal demonstrate that the metal's charge density exhibits deformations during light-matter interactions, emphasizing the necessity of considering the Lorentz degree of freedom and the number of electrons in the model.

In computer vision, a primary goal is to identify the location, orientation, and dimensions of objects within an image or scene. 3D object pose estimation has been the focus, but since object forms can greatly vary, predicting a complete 3D shape from an image is also challenging.  For instance, while a image might clearly show a car's shape, its shape is obscured in another image.  To tackle this, our research proposes an innovative approach that considers both 2D and 3D semantic keypoints for estimating a 3D object's pose and form.  Our method is exceptional because it is versatile, as it works with various geometric representations without needing any special properties.  Moreover, our method can handle instances where object forms are partially hidden in an image.  To test its robustness, our research implements a simulation to mimic real-world object deformations and demonstrates that our method can accurately estimate a 3D object's shape even in noisy and incomplete real-world settings.  Our method outperforms other approaches by a significant margin on the Category-level Object Pose Estimation Benchmark, particularly in cases with partially hidden objects.

This research establishes a method for creating confidence intervals and regions for random variables that follow a Cauchy distribution, taking into account both known and unknown parameters. A key aspect of this method involves employing a continuous version of the Haldane-Olkin transformation, which is combined with a non-parametric approach. Subsequent to obtaining the confidence intervals/regions, this method determines the probability that an estimate of a random variable lies within a particular interval in relation to the population parameter. Notably, this method offers a constant coverage rate for the confidence intervals/regions, as opposed to the traditional approach, which experiences a coverage rate of $2\alpha$ and varies according to the sample size. A thorough analysis is also conducted to compare the performance of the proposed method to the standard approach through the implementation of Monte Carlo simulations.

A new statistical method is developed for estimating sample sizes in basket trials with multiple subgroups. This is achieved by utilizing historical control data from each subgroup separately and combining them through a Bayesian approach to determine the required number of patients needed for future subsets in a basket trial. To facilitate this, a Dirichlet-convolution mixture model is developed as a unified tool for summarizing historical data across multiple subsets. A key innovation in this work involves the creation of a sample size formula that incorporates the uncertainty inherent in estimating subgroup response rates using only limited, pre-existing data. What emerges is a Bayesian formula for estimating the needed sample size per subgroup, where each subgroup's patient population is treated as a non-homogeneous Poisson process influenced by unknown parameters, for which a non-informative prior is established in conjunction with a Beta model for response rates. This framework allows researchers to obtain a lower bound for the required number of patients per subgroup in a basket trial, where each patient can belong to multiple subsets. To validate the proposed approach, several numerical examples are conducted, including a case study on treating cancer patients with multiple primary sites.

A cutting-edge approach known as SLS has emerged for the control of high-precision motion systems, involving the sequential closure of loops in a chain-like configuration. To further enhance performance, the SLS concept can be applied in a variable structure system that incorporates time-variant limitations and disturbances. However, the traditional SLS theory relies on the stability of the system's linearized form, which is problematic due to changes in the system's dynamic behavior. Therefore, a novel strategy based on the LPV-TSK fuzzy model is proposed to address this issue. The proposed method enables the derivation of a system that is close to stability, despite the presence of disturbances and within-defined limitations. Consequently, an improved control algorithm is developed, allowing for the execution of loop closures and effective system stabilization, outperforming the results obtained from the conventional SLS theory. Finally, simulation tests validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in terms of precision, robustness, and performance.

This paper introduces an innovative deep learning approach, partial-to-partial alignment using partial residual networks, specifically designed to handle alignment tasks involving incomplete and overlapping data points. Building upon the success of deep learning-based shape alignment, our method overcomes common limitations such as requiring a full and intact source shape and targets more practical applications like alignment of broken objects and mesh overlapping. To achieve this, we propose a new framework that uses partial residual networks to estimate missing information on the source shape's missing surfaces and surfaces not shared with the target shape. To enable supervision from partial surfaces, we suggest a patch-based comparison approach that uses individual patches of the source and target shapes as ground truth references. This allows the network to learn from each patch and guide the alignment process through local optimizations. Our method was tested and demonstrated effective results on alignment tasks involving fake and real shapes from various datasets.

We determine when the nilpotent quotients of a class of solvable group transformations have the $R_\infty$ property. Specifically, we investigate the nilpotent quotients of groups defined by automorphisms of the form $\phi_n(t) = t^{-1} (1 + t)^n$, focusing on the resulting nil-$\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$-modules and their relations to the $R_\infty$ property.

To evaluate the stability of the Standard Model, we compare theoretical forecasts for its instability at three particle colliders: the Future Circular Collider (FCC-e) electron collider, the International Linear Collider (ILC), and the Compact Linear Collider (CLIC). Considering the potential discoveries of four key physics processes, we assess the sensitivity of each collider to determine the instability. Assuming the mass of the Higgs boson to be 125 GeV, we find that the FCC-e, with its ability to produce a high-energy initial state, offers a significantly higher sensitivity to determine the instability, largely outweighing the capabilities of the ILC and CLIC.

Recent breakthroughs in optical excitation and manipulation of molecules have made it crucial to understand the detailed dynamics of molecular processes. Theoretical sturdy approaches to analyzing time-resolved data are needed to provide reliable and universal results, unaffected by assumptions and models. However, developing these approaches proves challenging due to the large amount of available data and the various models that could be applied. In this work, a universal method to analyze multidimensional time-resolved data is presented, employing a trajectory framework and a global optimization technique to provide a comprehensive description of molecular processes in their initial and final states. The method's reliability and versatility are validated by applying it to the well-documented case of NO$_2$ and interpreting the results in the context of existing knowledge on the molecule's dynamics.

To derive the density functions of $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons, the authors employ a novel approach using the Bethe-Salpeter wave functions. This involves the use of projection operators to define the density functions, followed by a calculation of the amplitude using the Bethe-Salpeter wave functions. This amplitude is then inserted into the field theoretic formulation of the bound state equations to obtain the density functions of $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons.

We investigate the behavior of Gelfand-Shilov spaces of smooth functions within the context of Fourier analysis. The properties of these spaces depend on the growth rates of their frequency and smoothness components. This work demonstrates that these spaces fall outside the category of Lebesgue spaces (Lp spaces) characterized by limited frequency growth. To establish this non-ordinary nature, we focus on the unique behavior of Toeplitz operators, which are linear transformations governed by window functions, and show that they conform to distinct types of linear operators depending on whether the Gelfand-Shilov spaces in question are ordinary or non-ordinary.

Deep learning methods have made significant advancements in semi-supervised learning, however, they still face challenges with instance-level tasks such as semantic segmentation, which requires a significant number of labeled samples, ultimately affecting model performance. To overcome this issue, researchers have made efforts to divide instances into meaningful groups based on their semantic characteristics, but most of these methods are limited to labeled data and are unable to efficiently partition instances across multiple modalities. To address this challenge, we propose a new cyclic division GAN architecture that learns to partition instances across multiple modalities without the need for explicit labels, effectively separating instances in a modalities-agnostic manner. Experimental results on three datasets - COCO-stuff, ADE20K, and Cityscapes - demonstrate that our method outperforms existing partitioning methods when provided with limited labeled data, while producing comparable results when labels are available in full.

This paper proposes a novel spatiotemporal action prediction framework using Gaussian Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernels to expand the contextual information of previous frames, a technique previously proven to be effective in support vector machine (SVM) classification, but not utilized in motion prediction. By utilizing RBF kernels to generate motion context, our model pre-trains a motion prediction network. The context is then incorporated into a main network, a variant of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory), for final motion prediction. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing methods on benchmark datasets for human action prediction.

On April 12, 1985, a massive outburst occurred from the red dwarf star AD Leo, producing an extraordinary amount of ultraviolet and visible energy that far exceeded its typical levels at the time, making it one of the largest stellar outbursts ever observed. We conducted a comprehensive simulation of this event by incorporating the properties of magnetic field dynamics and the interaction of high-speed coronal plasma streams. The outcomes of our analysis align closely with the observed data, highlighting the pivotal role of the coronal plasma streams in triggering such massive eruptions. Furthermore, our findings suggest that similar streams could potentially cause similar outbursts in other active red dwarf stars.

This research builds upon the work of Degeratu and Mathai by extending the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-structures. By adapting the method of Lanza-Eccheldano and Maschler for 7-manifolds with almost 3-subgroup structure, we have formulated the standard deformation theory of G2-instantons. We have also established that any G2-instanton deforms continuously to an arbitrary value of the L2-action. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that an abstract G2-instanton deforms if and only if its connection of non-compact type has a finite L2-norm. This general outcome supersedes the corresponding finding for 3-manifolds deforming G2-instantons in the light of 3-manifolds topologically equivalent to the three-fold product of the real lines, the circle, and the real lines. We have also explored the relationship between the L2-action and the L1-action, considered the deformation equation as an elliptic operator having an L2 L1-weights property, and proved that an G2-instanton deforms if its connection of non-compact type has a finite L1-norm. This general outcome supersedes the corresponding finding for 3-manifolds deforming G2-instantons. We have also established that an G2-instanton deforms continuously to an arbitrary value of the L1-action.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

We explore extensive compositions of natural numbers, examining their fundamental properties and establishing connections to random walks on the additive residue graph. Specifically, we analyze the vast compositions that lie within the core of other compositions, investigating their spectral properties and unique patterns that emerge under certain mod p transformations. These investigations lead to significant findings, revealing that the core compositions are uniquely defined and establishing the vast core compositions as optimal random walk strategies on the additive residue graph with a proven lower bound of λ1(ω) ≥ √(p-1)/2 for the largest eigenvalue.

In the realm of machine learning, the issue of inference bias has been a major concern, particularly when it comes to the representation of geometric data. One notable challenge emerges in the context of point cloud representations, where subtle variations in the geometric structure can pose significant difficulties for learning models. In our research, we introduce a novel technique called Transformation-Dependent Smoothing (TPC) to address these issues by optimizing the learning of geometric structure, thus enabling the development of accurate and robust models, even in the presence of uncertain and incomplete data. TPC can be seamlessly integrated into both learning and inference processes and demonstrates superior performance when compared to existing methods in a range of empirical evaluations, specifically in the context of 3D object categorization and detection applications.

This research investigates the performance of Frequency-Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar networks using ALOHA and CSMA access methods, focusing on ALOHA in its original and modified forms. Theoretical analysis and simulation results are obtained for both scenarios. For modified ALOHA, we find that the probability distribution of time between transmissions, no matter the interval, follows an exponential pattern as time approaches infinity. This contrasts with the initial ALOHA behavior where the distribution is not consistent. Additionally, we demonstrate that using a double-exponential model for packet arrival in the ALOHA analysis yields closer approximation to the simulated outcomes. Furthermore, comparing CSMA to the two variants of ALOHA reveals that employing a double-exponential model for packet arrival in the ALOHA analysis yields greater radar network capacity than CSMA.

Recent studies on entangled two-photon absorption have sparked interesting discussions on quantum optics, as they reveal a unique connection between entangled photon absorption and interference effects observed in the Hong-Ou-Mandel experiment. Building upon this interest, our analysis delves into a quantum model that combines these phenomena, utilizing a spectral analysis approach to better understand the relationships between these phenomena. By exploring various parameters, our findings demonstrate that distinct interactions between photons can influence the interference effects observed, as the interaction strength and entanglement of the photons impact the absorption rates and interference patterns.

We calculate the logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional vector spaces over the rational numbers, using the extended equivariant multiplicative reformulation of the M\"obius inversion principle. This formulation incorporates the Lefschetz fixed point theorem as its foundational method. By applying this method, we find that the rational circle action on CP(V) is a homotopy-class $K$-theory equivalence, allowing us to express the rational circle-equivariant $K$-theory of CP(V) in terms of the equivariant $K$-theory of the rational form of the Steinberg algebra $\mathscr{A}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{gl}_V)$. We employ this finding to determine the equivariant cohomology of the rational circle acting on CP(V)$^{\dim \mathscr{A}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{gl}_V)}$, which is equivalent to the equivariant cohomology of the rational form of the affine Grassmannian $\mathscr{A}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{gl}_V)$. We observe that this result enables us to express the logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of CP(V) in terms of the elliptic cohomology theory based on the Mukai dual of the moduli space of principal bundles over the rational form of the geometric invariant system $\mathbb{C

Building on the success of image and text classifications, the inference of temporal knowledge graphs has gained significant traction in developing effective knowledge graph embeddings. These embeddings, which convert knowledge graph data into a numerical format, have demonstrated impressive performance in knowledge graph completion tasks. In this research, we introduce a pioneering approach that utilizes only the subject and object rankings from existing knowledge graph embeddings without necessitating the generation of predicate rankings. These predicate rankings are usually obtained through supervised learning, which can be a time-consuming and costly endeavor. We achieve this by employing a data-driven method that focuses on the characteristics of low-ranking scores and demonstrating that high low-ranking scores encompass a substantial portion of data points, thereby rendering them sufficient for accurate inference results. Moreover, we propose a straightforward strategy to verify the validity of existing knowledge graph embeddings and show that these rankings can be effective in temporal knowledge graph inference without necessarily mimicking the rankings obtained through supervised learning.
Understandable Speech Perception in Noisy Environments

This study starts with a thorough examination of Bell nonlocality, its characteristics, and ways to demonstrate it, focusing on Bell inequalities and Bell nonlocality inequalities. An alternative method for verifying the existence of Bell nonlocality is explored without relying on inequalities. Instead, this alternative test ensures the generation of random variables that are not probabilistically equivalent to their classical counterparts, employing polytope-based non-convex regions, which serve as sufficient tests for Bell nonlocality. To facilitate practical applications, this method is further developed to conduct polytope-based tests using specific random variables obtained from polytope-based non-convex regions. Although the original goal is to showcase a non-locality without inequalities, this study also highlights the importance of understanding the non-locality without inequalities in the context of quantum systems, while also acknowledging that current research has primarily focused on its theoretical implications and highlighting the need for experimental verification through appropriate statistical analysis.

Flat bands, characterized by zero band gaps in the band structures of crystals, have garnered significant interest due to their inherent quantum conjugate systems and the presence of multiple Dirac cones. This fascination has led to the notion that flat bands are a unique feature among quantum systems, but historical examples from confined quantum wells have shown flat bands to be a normal occurrence. This understanding has been overlooked in the current literature on flat bands, perhaps due to a lack of familiarity with confined multiple particle systems or the use of band structures to describe collective behaviors. Nonetheless, the connection between flat bands in band structures and confinement is a fundamental concept in quantum physics that can be applied to various confinement scenarios, as seen in the multiple particle system where flat bands originate from the single particle states under confined conditions.

Researchers discovered that MB4 (M = Ca, Sr, Ba) compounds exhibit exceptional superconducting properties below 260 K, with the highest critical temperatures occurring in the barium version. Recent data suggest that MB4 materials are refined with a hexagonal inorganic network resembling graphite, but with significantly stronger interlayer attractions. This has led to speculation that hydrogen borides could possess even higher superconducting properties, potentially even exceeding those of magnesium diboride and iron-sehenide compounds. However, further analysis has uncovered that these speculations are unwarranted, with calculations indicating that the predicted superconductivity in these materials is not substantiated. In fact, the hydrogen borides do not exhibit the characteristic features typical of superconductors, with their behavior being dominated by very strong electric fields that contradict the phonon-mediated superconductivity typically observed in other materials. While the possibility of superconductivity in hydrogen-rich compounds cannot be entirely ruled out, it appears that the hydrogen borides do not possess this property, with their behavior being influenced by different physical mechanisms that result in very distinct characteristics compared to commonly observed superconductors.

A new concept known as static distribution analysis (SDA) is developed to
address the vacant thread issue and resource underutilization in simultaneous
multithreading systems, which are characterized by multiple cores sharing a
single instruction window. To achieve this, SDA evaluates program segments
graphically, identifying regions with potential execution overlap. The concept
is further explored through the introduction of a new mathematical operator for
distributing instructions across cores efficiently.

This study builds upon a prior paper by the same authors, expanding upon Charmability and Rigidity of Transformations in Teichmüller Space, specifically applying the concepts to arithmetic groups within Teichmüller space. The idea of charability is extended to include subgroups, such as $PSL(2,Z)$, and a key discovery shows that for certain groups, like $PSL(2,G)$ with a finite order, the concept of rigidity and charability becomes equivalent.

Highly automated driving systems can fail in special circumstances, and the industry is working to ensure that these systems can operate safely even when components fail. To achieve this, developers are creating systems that automatically switch to backup systems in case of failure, but this poses a major challenge as it is difficult to predict when such failures might occur. To establish the reliability of these systems, we conducted a formal verification of a fail-functional driving system, using a case study on a highly automated vehicle. The study focused on a system that detects and responds to camera failures on an vehicle, and this work has been recognized with a distinguished award at the ICSSE 2022 conference.

In the study of complex systems, such as weather and economic systems, clustering techniques are frequently used to group areas with similar characteristics. Currently, most clustering methods rely on predefined information about the systems they are analyzing, which is not the case with many real-world phenomena. Therefore, there is a need for more adaptive and data-driven clustering approaches that can identify meaningful groups in systems with limited available information. This paper presents an innovative algorithm called iBC, which uses the long-term dynamics of a system to determine similar sub-systems or states, ultimately leading to the creation of dynamic clusters. By applying this clustering method to two hypothetical systems and a realistic chaotical system, the researchers demonstrated its effectiveness and predicted its successful application in various fields, such as weather and campaign prediction.

This study offers an in-depth examination of the methodologies employed in Leibnizian infinitesimal analysis within the frameworks of Davis and Henson's nonstandard analysis, Katelin's big-O analysis, and also Tarski's real field with operator notation.

A growing method to study the large-scale structure of the universe uses HI intensity mapping technology in combination with interferometry. This method's accuracy will depend on how well its instrumental characteristics are understood, particularly the effects of its observational limitations. The present research utilizes a disturbance theory to model the effects of these limitations, specifically the impact of a spectrometer's 2D sampling pattern, and finds that its output can be represented by a cross-power spectrum between the HI density field and a weighted, mapped version of the field. The weighted map's kernel is determined by the spectrometer's sampling pattern. A more realistic model is then developed to account for the effects of the spectrometer's limited resolution and the HI intensity maps' line-width. This model's accuracy is verified through comparisons with simulation data. Our predictions suggest that the HI intensity mapping technique's accuracy will be influenced significantly by the spectrometer's sampling pattern, its resolution, and the HI intensity maps' line-width. Notably, the HI intensity mapping technique may provide better results using grids with higher density than the traditional pencil-beam surveys. Finally, our predictions suggest that the HI intensity mapping technique's accuracy will be able to correct for many of the instrumental effects associated with its observations, particularly when using grids with higher density.

A. A. P. Poulygin introduced the concept of autonomy for a difference operator with respect to a finite field, which he defined as the largest finite difference dimension. He demonstrated that this concept aligns with the traditional notion of infinity in various mathematical theories. Notably, he showed that a system of linear difference equations has solutions in an infinitely expanding space if and only if it has operator-based solutions involving an infinitely large number of frequencies. Building upon Poulygin's work, we extend the concept of autonomy to difference equations with coefficients that vary periodically. In this context, we establish a criterion for the existence of frequencies in such equations, linking it to the concept of Langlands dimension, which is a measure of non-diagonability in algebraic groups over finite fields.

Recent years have seen the widespread adoption of recommender systems, which have become an integral part of the digital landscape for numerous companies and individuals seeking to navigate the complex process of shaping user preferences. Among the numerous recommender technologies, collaborative filtering has consistently demonstrated exceptional accuracy and accuracy in modeling user behavior. Although it has significant limitations in addressing the data scarcity problem that plagues many industries, researchers have successfully merged their techniques with other methodologies to tackle this issue. This study specifically examines the potential benefits of integrating CF with natural language processing, highlighting the potential benefits of combining CF with NLP and NLP alone to improve user modeling. To this end, the authors presented an innovative, hybrid approach that merges the power of CF with NLP to generate context-driven and behavior-driven user profiles, thereby enhancing the accuracy of user context understanding and item recommendation. This novel method was tested using two actual real-world datasets and outperformed pure behavior-driven techniques, yielding impressive results, according to our experimental findings.

Wang and Zhou established the concept of freeness for random matrices, building upon earlier work by Bai and Wang. In this paper, we introduce a generalized definition of freeness, referred to as kind B freeness, and demonstrate its applicability to particular classes of random matrices, including those with eigenvalues and residual vectors. Additionally, we examine the relationship between kind B freeness and conditional independence for non-commutative polynomials, along with proving a centralized version of this concept, kind B central freeness.

For labeled transition systems with time, the dynamics of timed properties were previously explored by providing a straightforward characterization of all timed properties derived from basic ones, essentially describing a hierarchical structure. This paper reaffirms and adapts those findings in the context of branching time logic with time using a different characterization method and incorporates the advancements made since the initial publication.

Our previous study on the $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ process revealed that the process is heavily influenced by the $f_0(980)-a_0(980)$ resonance interplay. To build upon this finding, we conduct a comparative analysis of the $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta$ decay channel, examining its reaction dynamics in terms of the $\pi^0 \eta$ resonance and the $f_0(980)-a_0(980)$ resonance interplay. Our analysis shows that the direct $\pi^0 \eta$ decay contributes minimally, while the contribution from the $f_0(980)-a_0(980)$ resonance intertwining dominates the final quark composition of the hadron. As a result, the branching ratio of the $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta$ process is primarily determined by the $f_0(980)-a_0(980)$ resonance intertwining.

The GRAVITY instrument boasts four symmetrically aligned beams per pointing direction on the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI), allowing for a total of seven distinct entities in orthogonal directions - including a "capture" channel that operates in tandem with the primary feed. The purpose of this "capture" channel is to facilitate the offline realignment of the GRAVITY instrument and the capture of intricate dust structures via the polarization rotator system. The operational parameters of this "capture" channel have been examined in detail, with the focus on its capture power, the instrument's overall effect, and the residual off-line beam of the "capture" channel. The maintenance of a dedicated offline realignment and the captivity of the "capture" channel have been shown to be interchangeable, with the capture power determined by the position of the polarization rotator and the orientation of the "capture" channel's beam blockage mask. The analytical and numerical outcomes from a range of tests have been gathered, with the off-line realignment assessed via the offline realignment accuracy and a metric of the "capture" channel's effect, measured as the stabilized polarization ratio. The off-line realignment of GRAVITY can be performed with an accuracy of 0.2 degrees, and the "capture" channel's capture power is coupled with an off-line effect ranging from 0% to 70% of the instrumental's total effect. We examine the generalized k-center problem in graphs that may have non-planar topology. Their capacity to handle this issue depends heavily on the doubling properties of the underlying graph. We show that a particular class of graphs with limited doubling characteristics and high k values cannot be efficiently solved for finding the optimal solution using the standard approach based on the highway network method. To overcome this limitation, we propose an alternative algorithm that leverages a partitioning technique combined with the highway network method, allowing it to find the best solution for this specific graph class, even with high k values and limited doubling properties. We also extend this approach to apply to other efficient approximation algorithms for the generalized k-center problem. We develop a method to calculate the optimal value of the lambda parameter in our approach, which is critical for achieving the best results. We demonstrate the efficiency of this proposed algorithm by achieving the best known results for the generalized k-center problem with efficient doubling properties and also for the (generalized) k-center with efficient doubling characteristics under the L1 norm.

In this paper, we establish the following results for an entire function that meets specific criteria: if the difference between the number of times the function takes on positive values within a given square and the total area of those squares exceeds 3 times the function's logarithm to the power of the square of the square's side, multiplied by the square's side, plus 2, for all squares of a certain size, then the function is constant. Conversely, if the function is not constant, there exists a set of natural numbers where the difference between the number of times the function takes on positive values within a given square and the total area of those squares is less than the function's logarithm to the power of the square of the square's side, multiplied by the square's side, plus 1, for all squares of a certain size. Furthermore, if the difference between the number of times the function takes on positive values within a given square and the total area of those squares is less than the function's logarithm to the power of the square of the square's side, for all squares of a certain size, then there exists a set of natural numbers where the function takes on a positive value within that square.

This study introduces a novel complete solving method for polynomial equations of one variable, designed to work with systems that incorporate random errors of a specific type, ensuring a valid solution within a probabilistic framework. The algorithm was inspired by a probabilistic interpretation of the Subresultant algorithm and utilizes a new approach to eliminate variables one by one while controlling errors. We investigate the computational complexity of this method and compare it to other error-controlled solving methods, finding that it has a higher theoretical complexity than other approaches in some cases but is more versatile in terms of error modeling. Additionally, we show that by adopting an early termination strategy, the computational complexity of this method can be significantly reduced, making it more efficient in scenarios with a high probability of finding a solution and allowing for a trade-off between error tolerance and computational cost.

In a research project, it was discovered that emissions from bundles exhibit parity symmetry, which is protected by the total angular momentum and charge of the emitted photons. This project also identified the emission patterns of bundles under the impact of toroidal plasmon excitations in two-dimensional nanostructures. Furthermore, it was found that the intensity of emissions from charge-0 plasmons is solely dependent on the radial distance and the total angular momentum of the plasmons. This project used mode-resolved spectroscopy as an essential tool to study the parity symmetry of emissions from bundles.

A precise analytical model is presented, detailing the thermodynamic properties of equimolar binary alkali gas mixtures in terms of gas phase pressures and temperatures. This comprehensive model is substantiated by statistical mechanics and is accurate for all components, whether present in equilibrium or not. Formulas for equilibrium conditions are provided, along with simplified approximations for situations where species are very similar in mass. These models are substantiated through reliable numerical simulations based on path integral molecular dynamics and are validated with experimental data from the literature for gases like $^{87}$Rb-$^{85}$Rb and $^{133}$Cs-$^{133}$Cs.

In the context of a medium with a chiral discrepancy, we investigate the vector meson segment, deriving its in-medium Lagrangian from a model that incorporates the most fundamental constituents. The interaction between the vector mesons and the medium is represented by four quadratic form factors, two of which are connected to the chiral discrepancy and, therefore, vanish in a vacuum, while the other two form factors arise from the virtual virtual particles of the Rho and Omega mesons. The presence of the chiral discrepancy and the distinct virtual particles' contribution leads to a significant modification of the vector meson mass, as observed in experimental findings, where the Delta meson is notably unaffected.

We explore the fundamental issue of scale estimation in complex graphs affected by malicious activities. The scale of a graph refers to a measure of its size for purposes of determining whether a network is large or small. We develop two new algorithms for accurate scale estimation in graphs with a characteristic feature of smaller distances, despite the presence of an unknown bound on node malfunctioning nodes. Our first algorithm employs a predictive approach to estimate the scale of a graph with a linear complexity of n + poly(k) log n nodes, assuming an known bound on node malfunctions. If the bound on node malfunctions is unknown, we develop an algorithm based on density for large graphs with a complexity of n + poly(k) log n nodes. We prove the tightness of our results through a demonstration of lower bounds on the scale estimation algorithms of n poly(k) log n nodes. We validate the efficacy of our algorithms through successful implementation and testing on a range of datasets including a social network, a dataset of web page interactions and a deployment on a network of laptop nodes.

In numerical relativity, the advanced methods of Teukolsky, Chandra, and Taylor-Kevin (CTTK), are generally limited by data requirements rather than computational complexity. We introduce a new approach, also named CTTK, that facilitates the use of higher-order derivatives in the source terms, thereby enabling the management of data restrictions. We demonstrate that employing higher-order derivatives results in substantially improved inner boundary conditions, leading to notably increased stability for black-hole spacetimes. Consequently, CTTK's success allows the development of more efficient algorithms, needing neither rescaling nor conjugate gradient iterations to solve equations. We show that CTTK is compatible with a broad range of physical scenarios, including rotating black holes and black-hole neutron-star mergers, using the TeukNum relativity code.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves tracking the neutrino energy spectrum resulting from the $\beta\beta$-decay of $^{136}$Xe within a large liquid scintillator pool, surrounded by photomultiplier tubes. In order to assess their suitability for JUNO, comprehensive examinations were conducted on 320 20-inch PMTs, including electronic and photomagnetic characterization, magnetic filtering, and system functionality tests. The outcomes of these exams across multiple JUNO modules are presented here.

In practical scenarios like power consumption prediction and stock forecasting, long time series datasets often exhibit complex interconnected patterns that are difficult to model using traditional forecasting methods, leading to poor performance and inaccurate predictions that can result in significant financial losses, and in some cases, even lead to financial ruin. To address this challenge, a novel forecasting model called TimeFusedGCN is proposed, which effectively captures the spatial and temporal interdependencies in data by fusing the future and historical information in time series datasets through an innovative time-fusing mechanism, and an adaptive graph convolutional network structure optimization technique that automatically selects critical features and temporal dependencies for forecasting. To support the development of practical real-time forecasting applications, the model is designed with a high scalability of at most O(n^2) and can be trained on large datasets in a short time, with an average training speed of around 10-20 minutes. Experimental results show that TimeFusedGCN outperforms other models by providing significantly higher prediction accuracy with an average increase of 23.7% and 19.3% over ARIMA and ProPhES over a variety of numerical and categorical feature sets, and even achieves an impressive increase of 76.8% higher accuracy over ProPhES when using an adaptive feature selection approach, demonstrating its excellent real-world applicability and a great deal of potential for further model improvements.

In a previous study, our team made a groundbreaking discovery of a unique atmospheric phenomenon, now referred to as'scatter noise,' which significantly affects ground-based optical observations. This disturbance is caused by turbulent air currents in the high atmosphere, leading to flawed data across 6 to 20 micrometers in space-based observations and ground-based measurements taken with a telescope of greater altitude than the atmospheric layer it's operating within. To further comprehend'scatter noise' and make'scatter noise-free' observations possible, we've developed two empirical models, which will be explained in detail, along with the reasoning behind them. Our mission is to eventually make'scatter noise' a constant of the past, and to do this, we're developing a novel algorithm that utilizes data from the Mauna Kea summit to constantly monitor the'scatter noise' and make'scatter noise'-free observations possible.

Recently, pre-trained language models have been used to label data for other tasks,  making data annotation more efficient. However, the quality of these labels can be unreliable  due to the inconsistencies of the 0-1 and multi-class labels provided by the large teams of human annotators.  To resolve this, we propose a new approach, PILE, which utilizes the logits from a ensemble of human labels to accurately remove incorrect examples during the training process.  Through PILE's use, the model can effectively focus on the well-labeled examples and make training more robust against poor human annotations.  Our approach outperforms other distillation methods on multiple datasets and demonstrates the significance of human annotation quality in shaping model performance.

The current model of the universe's makeup, based on a decade of observations with spacecraft and ground-based telescopes, suggests that an unknown dark matter component may exist, making up approximately thirty percent of total matter and radiation combined. To further understand this unknown component, scientists have proposed the use of dark matter-sensitive detectors as a valuable research tool. A hypothetical system consisting of two particles, one of which is an ultralight dark matter particle, is proposed in this research. The detectors used in this study are hypothetical microscopic capacitors, where a short-lived state known as a 'dark cup' forms when the ultralight particle is captured between the capacitor's plates, giving rise to a detectable resonance frequency. The resonance frequency is found to be directly proportional to the mass of the ultralight particle, while its width is influenced by various factors such as decay and leakage. The resulting frequency-mass relationship, influenced by the particle's lifetime and moisture content, offers researchers a valuable range of options to further investigate the properties of this enigmatic matter type. The study demonstrates that the characteristics of ultralight dark matter can be accurately identified through a specific set of conditions, collective motion patterns, and specific spectral patterns.

This study confirms the singular uniqueness of solutions to basis pursuit using a direct approach, analyzing the problem through the lens of measureability and the generation of measures through optimization. Alongside this, we demonstrate the large-scale, smooth, differentiable nature of the basis pursuit solution set and explore its general applicability to the family of linearly constrained optimization problems.

P416 is a promising match-action table switch architecture that can efficiently process complex flow entries through its hierarchical template-matching structure. Currently, compiling P416 program(s) into configurable match-action tables remains an unresolved issue due to the challenges posed by template-matching-based programs. This study proposes an open-source, C++-based compiler framework for P416 programs, enabling direct compilation to fixed-size match-action tables. The compiler's efficiency can be optimized by utilizing a cache to avoid recursive template-matching operations. We evaluated our compiler using open-source P416 benchmarks and compared it with existing P416 compilers, demonstrating that our compiler produces the most efficient match-action tables with the shortest compilation times.

This study focuses on the vector conveyance equation, a novel model for porous media flows that accounts for conveyance in addition to permeability. To improve the spatial approximation, a fully non-discrete, high-accuracy Galerkin discretisation is formulated using the RT0 elements, yielding exceptionally precise results. Nevertheless, this method's computational expense is extremely high. To find a balance between accuracy and efficiency, we analysed the conveyance tensor's asymptotic properties near singular points and established a theoretical error estimate for the conventional and our newly proposed discretisation methods. Numerical trials confirmed that the predicted error rates closely match the theoretical estimates. Notably, the proposed method's error rate is only one degree higher than the theoretical maximum, making it exceptionally reliable.

Federated Learning aims to facilitate the global exchange of personal data, enabling collaborative model development among geographically dispersed entities while maintaining local data privacy. This can be achieved by utilizing Differential Privacy on client-side data, where the owners of private datasets contribute to global model training by submitting anonymized data. Theoretical justifications for FL's privacy benefits have been established but lack substantiation in empirical analysis. This paper addresses this gap by performing the first comprehensive examination of DP-Federated Learning, focusing on various deployment strategies, network capabilities, and dataset characteristics. Our investigation highlights the tension between global model accuracy and client data privacy, showing that current implementations fall short in balancing these competing demands. Specifically, we found that the majority of test cases experience a noticeable increase in generalization errors due to overfitting, indicating a failure to accurately capture data diversity. Our findings suggest that the current paradigm is inadequate and that alternative methods are required to address the complexities of Federated Learning deployment, particularly in contexts where data owners are involved in the training process.

Researchers analyzed data from the BESIII detector, which operates at BEPCII, in a search for the $B_c^+(1480)$ meson. The investigation involved looking at the $B_c^+(1480) \to J/\psi \pi^+$ decay channel. To validate the search, the team used a statistical method called the unbinned maximum likelihood method. As a result, the analysis discovered the $B_c^+(1480)$ meson, which has a mass of $4787.0^{+8.4}_{-7.6}\pm 3.1$ MeV, along with a branching fraction of $4.2^{+3.4}_{-1.7}\pm 0.6%$ relative to the $B_c^+(1S) \to J/\psi \pi^+$ decay channel. The analysis also provided upper limits on the $B_c^+(1480)$ meson's branching fractions for two other decay channels: $B_c^+(1480) \to B^+ \phi$ and $B_c^+(1480) \to B_s^+ \phi$.

Runge-Kutta estimation methods have been highly effective in tracking states and misalignments in various applications, but traditional implementations have been limited to discrete input data with unknown noise levels. To address this limitation, a new continuous-phase Runge-Kutta estimation algorithm has been developed, allowing the use of theoretical noise models and time-dependent inputs to improve accuracy. The proposed approach employs a continuous-time formulation, incorporating the statistical properties of noise in differential equations to provide a reliable solution. The algorithm was validated through simulations of a simple pendulum and a nonlinear coupling system, demonstrating its superiority over traditional estimation techniques.

When training neural networks using large datasets, model-parallel training can significantly speed up the process by distributing the workload across multiple GPUs, but it comes with the drawback of limited model size due to communication costs. This paper focuses on developing an innovative technique to increase the maximum allowed model size for parallel training by evaluating the effects of regional loss calculations and error propagation on deep neural networks. We thoroughly analyzed the current standards of error propagation and introduced an enhanced approach to reduce communication overhead, ultimately demonstrating an efficient solution for training highly complex neural networks in a distributed environment with minimal loss accuracy.

Three-dimensional chaotic systems that scatter particles show unique characteristics when the obstacle's surface has complex properties. This is especially true for areas near Wada basins, which transition smoothly between separating and interconnected regions when the obstacle's shape changes slightly. However, the impact of dissipative forces on these basins and their associated transition phenomena remains largely unexplored. By combining numerical and mathematical approaches, researchers have studied how a weak level of dissipation affects three-dimensional chaotic scattering systems with complex surfaces. Their study reveals that small amounts of dissipation can actually increase the efficiency of scattering and alter the system's phase transitions, including those involving Wada basins. Notably, this is true for both conservative and dissipative systems, which has important implications for scattering phenomena and surface transitions in physics and biology.

The interplay of quantum interactions among light and matter remains a rich area of study. A concrete example of its potential influence comes from modifying the electromagnetic force's characteristics, which can lead to novel phenomena such as the creation of bosons that interact with taste. Considering the large disparity in energy scales between the taste boson and the Planck boson suggests that direct production through particle collisions may be challenging. As an alternative, exploring the taste boson's potential impact on baryogenesis or the creation of stable particles with non-standard properties within various low-energy frameworks is a more viable approach. A preliminary examination within the framework of the mirror matter model indicates that taste bosons can evolve into mirror bosons, leading to the creation of stable particles with repulsive forces. Furthermore, the possibility of taste bosons facilitating the creation of mirror dark matter is also explored.

In daily life, people frequently encounter scenarios involving an intense focus on a single activity, but surrounding activities may also provide contextual insights, improving overall performance. To optimize recognition, it's practical to assume that nearby moments, akin to a "buffer zone," holding similar information, should be considered. Thus, a more comprehensive approach involves identifying the primary activity and utilizing a buffer zone consisting of consecutive clips. Both the primary activity and buffer zone can be analyzed using a focused network, where each node represents an activity and the directed edge towards another node indicates the likelihood of the mentioned activity. To address this, we propose the Hierarchical Focus Network (HiFocus), consisting of a layer that identifies the active activities and a secondary level that makes targeted predictions for each identified activity. For each activity, the associated "buffer zone" predictions are combined to yield a more comprehensive prediction. As there's limited existing research on this topic, we create an artificial dataset called "Focus-10" comprising 10 diverse activities and a complex scenario with overlapping temporal ranges to validate the efficacy of our proposed model. Experimental results confirm that HiFocus produces a robust prediction for a given timeline by focusing on the "buffer zone" associated with each identified activity.

This research investigates the thermodynamic behavior of Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes accompanied by a scalar field, examining the impact on the thermodynamic system when the scalar field meets specific criteria and analyzing the implications for the weak cosmic censorship hypothesis.

Investigating the fundamental process of star formation using theoretical models is complicated by the lack of observational evidence directly linking protostars to their parent molecular clouds. To address this, a new approach focuses on the relationship between the relative abundance of certain isotopes in the sun and the characteristics of star-forming regions, which provides a viable proxy for the clouds' initial composition. Based on this theory, a numerical model is developed to analyze the early stages of star formation. The results of this model reveal a previously predicted relationship between the star's mass and the distance between the star and the center of the cloud, as well as the star's speed and its surrounding accretion disk mass. Additionally, the model provides an explanation for the observed mass disparity between the star and the cloud, resolving a long-standing astrophysical puzzle.

This paper presents a novel method to compute thermodynamic quantities and entropy using Nested Sampling, allowing for approximation at any level of precision. To achieve this, we reframe Nested Sampling as a Monte Carlo integration technique, evaluating the integrand only when its value surpasses the current boundary. This realization leads to two distinct approaches for calculating entropies, which are discussed in detail along with a proposed method for estimating thermal phase transitions. The proposed algorithm necessitates only a single evaluation of the wave function and its derivatives, thereby facilitating its integration into existing NS codes with minimal modifications.

We investigate a particular type of conservation law involving a feeble solution in a highly complex setting. Building on the work of Di Pillo with Bressan and Han, we extend the existing theory to include situations where the solution is not necessarily smooth or weakly continuous. In addition, we develop a unique construction method for feeble solutions in situations where solutions may not exist as long-term or short-term solutions.

Cyberattacks on IoT devices are expanding at an alarming rate, fueled by their exposed network connections and basic security measures. As a result of the widespread use of Naive Bayes classifiers in detecting network assaults, we noticed a notable increase in their effectiveness in this field. To take advantage of the strengths of convolutional neural networks and their ability to interpret complex network patterns, we developed a Naive Bayes classifier layer. The introduction of this layer enables Naive Bayes classifiers to leverage the benefits of CNNs without requiring the acquisition of significant computational resources. The proposed Naive Bayes classifier achieved competitive accuracy compared to leading CNN-based competitors, showcasing its superiority in resource-constrained devices. The source code for this project is available at: https://github.com/AbdelrahmanAbouElEnein/NBcoded.

If a group G acts on a set X by permutations, an action of G is considered soluble if the group is soluble. We define the number of G-actions on X that yield soluble groups as the soluble activities, denoted by $A_s(X, G)$. In this context, our research explores the similarities and differences between $A_s(X, G)$ and the total number of G-actions on X, $A(X, G)$. Notably, we demonstrate that $A_s(X, G)$ is equal to the sum of all $A_s(\Xi, H)$, where the pairs $(\Xi, H)$ comprise isomorphic images of $(X, G)$. Furthermore, we establish a direct relationship between $A_s(X, n) and the total number of G-actions on X, $A(x, n)$. We further investigate how $A_s(X, n)$ behaves in relation to the order of G. Additionally, we look into the case of faithful actions, examining the relationship between $A_{sf}(X, n)$ and the order of G.

Animal movement patterns hold significant value in ecological research. Analyzing video footage allows researchers to focus on individual animals, but their automatic identification within large datasets remains a significant challenge. Existing methods, including those that utilize deep learning, lack flexibility when working with limited annotated information. To address this, we've developed a novel approach for identifying and tracking individual animals in videos, even when only a single image is available for annotation. Our network's performance is particularly impressive, with higher accuracy rates compared to the current best-performing methods, as evident from our experimental results. Additionally, our findings show that a well-trained model can effectively identify and track animals in videos with minimal to no noise, while also detecting multiple animals in a single frame.

This research outlines a proposed method to optimize the efficiency of energy networks by utilizing quantum computing resources to conduct complex optimization tasks. We have developed a quantum algorithm that can identify the most cost-effective solutions for managing energy supply and demand by dynamically adjusting the power output of energy plants. To achieve optimal results, we have developed a specific quantum strategy involving the adjustment of energy production levels through the application of unitary operators. To address variabilities in energy demand, a hybrid approach combining quantum and classical computing techniques is proposed to determine the most suitable power output levels. This method involves the iterative use of quantum computing for general optimization and classical computing for specific adjustments to meet changing energy demands. We have verified the effectiveness of this hybrid method through numerical simulations that utilized the HOAQ library to implement the proposed algorithm on a quantum circuit simulator.

This research explores how physical laws can be inferred from probabilistic constraints, focusing on nonlocality as a crucial factor. The study introduces a framework to analyze the consistency of these laws and examines the inherent inconsistencies resulting from their inherent nonlocality. A concrete example is provided by the quantum mechanical context in which the laws of blackbody radiation and entropy are revealed to be interconnected with nonlocality, yet the laws of thermodynamics, which rely on entropy, reveal a contradictory nature stemming from the constraints of nonlocality. A possible pathway to resolve this contradiction and potentially unlock a new understanding of physical laws is also discussed.

This study seeks to identify long-lasting, large-scale ionizers moving quickly. The research utilized the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider in pp collisions with a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy. The analysis considered the entire dataset from two periods of data collection, adding up to 139 inverse femtobarns of integrated luminosity. The study focuses on tracks with notable energy loss and long-lasting signals from the inner detector and the muon chambers. The study further differentiates these signals from background, using the concentration of primary interaction particles, the trajectory of charged particles, and other factors. The study does not reveal any significant anomalies above the predicted background, and the results are translated into 95% and 84% confidence levels. The study sets new standards at one specific energy loss level, specifically 5 GeV for heavy particles weighing around 700 GeV. The study explores the relationship between the mass of particles and their charge-to-mass ratio, with the lower limits on the cross-section of certain interactions also being explored in this study.

We have developed a highly advanced on-chip single-photon device using highly sensitive silicon photonic structure technology. The system leverages a combination of linear and nonlinear optical functions in integrated circuits to achieve cutting-edge spectral selectivity, high emission rates, and exceptionally low optical loss levels. By incorporating cutting-edge microheater technology that utilizes nanoscale resistance for efficient heat dissipation, we have surpassed the 99% efficiency mark in a 1 km long silicon circuit, showcasing a notable advancement in the field. The breakthrough achieves notable enhancement in the overall performance of the on-chip single-photon device, bringing it closer to the theoretical limit for photonics in the low-frequency range.

Neutron spin flip and inelastic scattering experiments were conducted on
intact samples of different species, specifically raccoon dogs and mice, to
obtain dual insights into their temperature-dependent metabolic processes and
the animals' weight distribution of neutrons. The goal was to understand how
the animals' metabolic activities are linked to their size and movement.
Initial results from the experiment revealed the presence of a boson summit,
characterized by a boson ratio that increases with temperature, indicating a
correlation between temperature and the animals' movement. Further
experiments using a higher-resolution setup confirmed the boson summit and
showed that its boson ratio is influenced by the species and their movement.
Notably, the boson ratio of mice was found to be higher than that of raccoon
dogs, even though the mice have a lower average weight. The experiment's dual
outcomes provided a deeper understanding of the boson summit and its relation to
the animals' movement, while also validating the use of neutron scattering
as a means of studying metabolic processes.

Particle physics is becoming a complex system to model theoretically, making it crucial to set aside simplicity in favor of precise calculations based on observed data. Advanced computer programs can now evaluate complex mathematical expressions with high precision, but their underlying theories rely on outdated assumptions regarding how particles interact. A new framework is being developed to address this issue by utilizing cutting-edge mathematical concepts, specifically involving geometric relationships. Although the proposed system involves complex mathematical expressions, its intricate nature can be broken down into simpler components, making it feasible to implement in computer programs. A prototype implementation of this new framework has already shown promising results in evaluating complex mathematical expressions with high precision.

The ability of a system to absorb energy is connected to the availability of specific pathways, known as eigenchannels, that facilitate the transfer of energy into the system. These eigenchannels can be characterized in various frameworks, such as scattering matrix eigenstates, S-matrices, and transfer matrices. Each framework offers unique insights, but they share important similarities, as we will establish in this study by deriving key relationships among these matrices and eigenchannels. Notably, we demonstrate that the number of effective eigenchannels across different frameworks is interrelated and bound by a comprehensive principle: the Karovich-Loewner-Vinberg theorem. Consequently, this study provides an essential framework for understanding the system's capacity to absorb energy, as characterized by the number of effective eigenchannels in each framework, and establishes the notion of "channels" and "mirrors" to describe these pathways.

Researchers have uncovered a previously undiscovered spiral feature in the center of the Milky Way, located 3,000 parsecs from the galaxy's core in the direction of the constellations of Sagittarius and Scorpius. This newly identified arm, named the 3-Kpc Hook, appears to be a fresh, thin spiral section based on the analysis of the Galactic Center Star Survey and the VVVX brown dwarf catalog using a machine learning algorithm. This algorithm's results show that the 3-Kpc Hook shares similar characteristics with the central spiral arms of the Milky Way, such as metallicity, luminosity distribution, and proper motion, indicating that it is likely part of the Milky Way's spiral structure. However, further research is needed to confirm the 3-Kpc Hook's origin and its place within the galaxy's overall framework.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover comprehensive solutions, addressing various limitations of conventional methods that often yield only a single optimal solution. To meet these needs, researchers have developed algorithms that can explore multiple optimal solutions, potentially leading to more efficient operations in areas like supply chain management and resource allocation. A key aspect of these algorithms revolves around phenotypic variety, measuring the extent of exploration in the solution space, guided by phenotypic fitness, to distinguish suitable solutions. However, the effectiveness of phenotypic variety is largely supported by theoretical background rather than substantial evidence. To refine our understanding, this study examines the correlation between phenotypic variety and multi-solution optimization, analyzing its impact on various domains, including multi-objective, multi-attribute, and supply chain optimization, to provide insights into its application and potential value.

We're examining a stable matching scenario where agents form long-term relationships, similar to marriages, with two individuals sharing living space. Our 'Houseymoon Problem' involves dealing with a 3D stable matching dilemma, where agents have unique and varied preferences for potential partners and roommates. Our investigation focuses on whether having complete, distinct, and overlapping preferences suffices for ensuring the existence of stable and almost stable matches. To answer this question, we'll need to make progress towards resolving an open problem concerning stable matches with one-dimensional preferences.

We carry out first-principles operations on the valley excitation spectra of electron-phonon coupling in two-dimensional materials. The results show that when the interaction between electrons and phonons is significant, the valley dynamics changes due to the modification of the interaction mechanism from a conventional type to a nonlocal one. The presence of an innovative interaction mechanism leads to the emergence of an innovative phonon band, which is located near the ultraviolet ultra-violet ultra-violet ultra-violet ultra-violet ultra-violet ultra-violet ultra-violet ultra-violet ultra-violet ultra-violet ultra-violet ultra-violet ultra-violet ultra-vited. The innovative phonon band's width is influenced by the interaction mechanism's type, indicating that the valley dynamics is closely tied to the phonon band's shape. The valley dynamics' unique characteristics can be controlled by adjusting the phonon band's shape, which is in turn influenced by the innovative interaction mechanism.

This research introduces the concept of "purity" in the Gromov-Hausdorff distance, establishing its relationship with categories having subcategories isomorphic to the real numbers. Purity in this context is also connected to the non-purity of certain operators on directed systems. Additionally, the study characterizes certain types of subcategories that can be found in any given category with a non-pure structure. Specifically, it has been shown that these subcategories must include intervals, or what is equivalently, real lines that can be embedded within the original category.

This paper introduces a microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with an extremely wide bandwidth. The antenna's microstrip-fed patch is coupled to a circular slot on the same board, which acts as a resonant patch to contribute to the antenna's radiating characteristics. To achieve a broad angular coverage, the antenna's microstrip-fed patch is also coupled to an elliptical patch via a shorting post, which acts as a quarter-wavelength transformer. The combination of these two patches enables the antenna to provide a broad bandwidth and wide beamwidth, allowing it to operate at mm-waves (above 10 GHz) with a broad bandwidth (greater than 10%) and a wide beamwidth (exceeding 60 degrees), which is a rare feature in antennas at mm-waves. The antenna's simulated center frequency is around 28 GHz, with a broad bandwidth ranging from 25.2 GHz to 29.7 GHz, and a wide beamwidth of 62 degrees. The antenna's measured results show that its bandwidth and beamwidth closely match its simulated values.

The commercialization of quantum computing is hindered by the reliability issues of current quantum processors, prone to systematic and random errors. To overcome these limitations, researchers have developed quantum error correction using multiple fault-free paths to data, a technique supported by the fault-free code theory. Building upon this concept, a novel approach employs reinforcement learning to create fault-free coders. The coder's codebook is initialized randomly, and through the exchange of classical messages with the decoder, it selects the most suitable codeword to transmit when sending quantum information over an unreliable channel. The decoder, also utilizing reinforcement learning, optimizes the decoding process by adapting the decoder's codebook in response to the receiver's observations. The efficacy of this method has been successfully tested in a recent study using the quantum register of ions and found to approach the theoretical maximum in high noise conditions.

Quantum-enhanced metrology uses the quantum properties of matter and light to increase the precision of physical measurements, surpassing classical limitations. This is achieved through techniques such as entanglement, using non-classical states and specific interactions to make precise measurements. The connection of multiple cavities allows for the exploration of complex quantum systems and potentially applications in optical networks for parameter estimation. However, the quantum properties of this system are challenged by losses, preventing the implementation of highly precise measurements. The present research focuses on the quantum properties of a double-cavity system with an atom, where an applied laser has variable characteristics. The results indicate that even with losses, the quantum properties of the system can still be utilized for highly precise measurements, enabled by the entanglement of the lost and remaining photons. This is exemplified by the increased precision of measurements of similar parameters.

This study examines photons produced at central and mid-peripheral regions in 200 GeV Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions through measurement of direct photon-hadron correlations. The observations are supported by a basic model of photon production and it suggests that the response of the medium to quarks and gluons is similar in Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions. The relationships between the photon-hadron correlations and the properties of the medium formed in these collisions remain to be further explored.

To evaluate the performance of the hybrid digital-analog quantum computing method for simulating fermionic systems, we compared its results with those obtained from the fermionic quantum phase space method. Both methods yielded identical outcomes for the expected values of certain observables, which were computed using a quantum state obtained by simulating the interacting fermionic system via the Jordan-Schwinger representation. Notably, the hybrid digital-analog method and the fermionic quantum phase space method performed equally well, with the latter exhibiting exponential scalability in the number of fermions and degrees of freedom. We carried out simulations for two- and three-dimensional systems with varying numbers of fermions and examined how the coefficients of the Taylor expansions of the energy, momentum, and Wigner eigenfunctions impacted their computational complexity.

A fundamental issue in machine learning has evolved into a critical problem, where models excel in optimized solutions but struggle with generalization. This paper explores a new approach to address this challenge by employing wealthly attributes, which produce efficient solutions with strong generalization capabilities. The proposed method is examined through experiments with multiple benchmark problems, featuring a unique evaluation framework that assesses both candidate solutions and wealthly attributes to evaluate performance. Our results indicate that wealthly attributes produce high-quality solutions, outperforming alternative strategies, including the use of distilled attributes to mitigate the generalization gap.

The effectiveness of optical trapping in manipulating biological and organic materials has prompted a search for a suitable spatial light modulator to control light distribution and interaction with these materials, leading to a proposed new concept based on a fuzzy logic control system to optimize its performance along with traditional phase encoding.
